subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 4! In this unit you will become fluent and confident with decimals and the four operations you can perform on them: ordering and comparing, adding and subtracting, multiplying and dividing. You will also learn a set of clever mental strategies that let you calculate quickly in your head, and you will use all of these skills to solve real problems drawn from markets, measurement, sport and science.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics 0862 — Stage 7 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Explain the place value of any digit in a decimal number, including tenths, hundredths and thousandths.
Compare and order decimals with different numbers of decimal places using place value.
Add and subtract decimals by lining up the decimal points correctly.
Multiply decimals and place the decimal point using the decimal-places rule.
Divide decimals, including dividing by a decimal by converting to whole-number division.
Use mental strategies – rounding and adjusting, fraction equivalents, partitioning, and compensation – to calculate efficiently.
Estimate to check whether a calculated answer is sensible.
Solve multi-step word problems involving decimals and interpret the answers in context.
Add and subtract positive and negative decimals, including numbers with a different number of decimal places, by combining the sign rules with the decimal-point method.

concepts.title: Decimal Place Value
concepts.explanation:
Every decimal skill rests on place value – the system that gives meaning to the position of each digit. In our number system each place is worth ten times the place to its right. The decimal point marks the boundary between the whole-number places on the left and the fractional places on the right.

Take the number 3456.789. Reading from the left: the 3 is in the thousands place (3 × 1000 = 3000), the 4 is in the hundreds (400), the 5 is in the tens (50), and the 6 is in the ones (6). After the point the pattern continues, but now each place is a tenth of the one before: the 7 is in the tenths place (7 × 0.1 = 0.7), the 8 is in the hundredths (8 × 0.01 = 0.08), and the 9 is in the thousandths (9 × 0.001 = 0.009).

This structure explains why 0.5 is greater than 0.05. In 0.5 the 5 sits in the tenths place, so it is worth 5 × 0.1 = 0.5. In 0.05 the 5 sits in the hundredths place, so it is worth only 5 × 0.01 = 0.05. Because a tenth is ten times bigger than a hundredth, 0.5 is ten times bigger than 0.05. Getting this idea firmly in your mind now will save you from the single most common decimal mistake.

Place value also explains why you may add trailing zeros without changing a number. The number 2.5 can be written 2.50 or 2.500, because adding zeros in the hundredths and thousandths places adds nothing – they represent 0 hundredths and 0 thousandths. Writing 2.5 as 2.500 does not change its value, but it does show the number to greater precision, which is useful when you line up decimals for adding or subtracting.

You can always break a decimal into the sum of its place values. For example, 0.375 means 3 tenths + 7 hundredths + 5 thousandths, which is 3/10 + 7/100 + 5/1000. Writing all three over a common denominator gives 300/1000 + 70/1000 + 5/1000 = 375/1000, which simplifies to the fraction 3/8. Seeing decimals and fractions as two faces of the same number is a powerful habit.
concepts.example: Finally, strong place-value intuition helps you estimate and check. If you are working out 23.7 × 4.8, you know the answer must be near 24 × 5 = 120. So an answer of 1137.6 or 11.376 would immediately warn you that the decimal point has been misplaced. Estimating the size of an answer before you calculate is one of the best error-catching habits in all of mathematics.

concepts.title: Ordering and Comparing Decimals
concepts.explanation:
To compare decimals, work through the place values from left to right, starting with the largest place. Stop as soon as one number has a bigger digit in a place where the other is smaller. This systematic method works no matter how many decimal places the numbers have.

Compare 3.45 and 3.7. The ones digits are both 3, so move on. In the tenths place, 3.45 has 4 tenths while 3.7 has 7 tenths. Since 7 > 4, we conclude 3.7 > 3.45 – even though 3.45 looks longer. The number of digits does not decide the size; the place values do.

When numbers have different numbers of decimal places, it helps to add trailing zeros so every number has the same length. To compare 2.8 and 2.75, rewrite 2.8 as 2.80. Now line them up: 2.80 and 2.75. The ones and tenths match at 2 and 8 versus 2 and 7 – wait, look carefully: tenths are 8 versus 7, so 2.80 > 2.75. Making the lengths equal removes the confusion completely.

To order several decimals, apply the same comparison to the whole set. Put 4.23, 4.6 and 4.179 in order from smallest to largest. All three have 4 in the ones place, so look at the tenths: 4.23 has 2, 4.6 has 6, and 4.179 has 1. Since 1 < 2 < 6, the order is 4.179, 4.23, 4.6. A neat trick is to write each number to the same number of decimal places first – 4.230, 4.600, 4.179 – which makes the comparison almost automatic.

Beware of two traps. First, leading and trailing zeros behave differently. The numbers 0.45 and 0.045 are not the same: 0.45 is 45 hundredths while 0.045 is 45 thousandths, so 0.45 is ten times larger. But 2.5, 2.50 and 2.500 are all equal, because trailing zeros after the last non-zero digit add nothing. Second, do not compare by counting digits: a learner might wrongly think 0.8 < 0.75 because 75 looks bigger than 8. Written as 0.80 and 0.75, it is clear that 80 hundredths beats 75 hundredths, so 0.8 > 0.75.
concepts.example: A number line makes ordering visual. On a line from 2 to 3, the number 2.3 sits a little past the start while 2.7 sits closer to the end. Because 2.7 is further to the right, 2.7 > 2.3. Real life is full of decimal ordering: comparing the prices $12.45, $12.4 and $12.54 to find the cheapest, or ranking three race times to find the fastest runner. In every case, line up the place values and compare carefully.

concepts.title: Adding and Subtracting Decimals
concepts.explanation: Adding and subtracting decimals follows the same idea as with whole numbers, with one golden rule: line up the decimal points. This makes sure you add tenths to tenths, hundredths to hundredths, and so on. Filling any gaps with trailing zeros keeps every column the correct length. To work out 23.45 + 7.8, write the numbers with points aligned and add a trailing zero to 7.8 so both have two decimal places: These same steps also work when a decimal is negative. First line up the decimal points (padding with trailing zeros so every number has the same number of decimal places), then use the same sign rules you use for negative whole numbers: adding a negative is the same as subtracting, and subtracting a negative is the same as adding. For example, to work out −3.6 + 1.25, first pad −3.6 to −3.60. Since the signs are different, subtract the smaller size from the larger and keep the sign of the larger: 3.60 − 1.25 = 2.35, and because 3.60 is negative, the answer is −2.35.
concepts.example: Start from the right. Hundredths: 5 + 0 = 5. Tenths: 4 + 8 = 12, so write 2 and carry 1 into the ones column. Ones: 3 + 7 + 1 (carried) = 11, so write 1 and carry 1 into the tens. Tens: 2 + 1 (carried) = 3. The answer… Another example: 4.2 − 7.85. Rewrite 4.2 as 4.20, and think of it as 4.20 + (−7.85). The signs are different, so subtract the smaller size from the larger: 7.85 − 4.20 = 3.65, and because 7.85 is the larger size and it is negative, the answer is −3.65.

concepts.title: Multiplying Decimals
concepts.explanation:
Multiplication of decimals combines ordinary multiplication with one clear rule for the point: the number of decimal places in the answer equals the total number of decimal places in the two numbers you multiplied. This rule works every time, however complicated the numbers.

To find 2.3 × 1.4, ignore the points and multiply 23 × 14 = 322. Now count decimal places: 2.3 has one, 1.4 has one, so the answer needs 1 + 1 = 2 decimal places. Place the point to give 3.22. Check by estimating: 2.3 × 1.4 is about 2 × 1.4 = 2.8, so 3.22 is sensible.

For 0.25 × 0.6, multiply 25 × 6 = 150. The factors have 2 + 1 = 3 decimal places, so the answer is 0.150, which we write as 0.15. Notice that multiplying by a number less than 1 makes the result smaller than you started with – taking 0.6 of something gives you less than the whole. This surprises many learners, but it makes sense: 8 × 0.3 = 2.4, because you are taking only three tenths of 8.

When one number is a whole number, the rule still holds. For 4 × 2.35, multiply 4 × 235 = 940. Only 2.35 has decimal places (two), and 4 has none, so the answer has 2 + 0 = 2 decimal places: 9.40 = 9.4. For numbers with many places, such as 2.345 × 1.67, multiply 2345 × 167 = 391615, then count 3 + 2 = 5 decimal places to get 3.91615.
concepts.example: Multiplying decimals appears constantly in real life. The area of a rectangular garden 4.5 m long and 2.8 m wide is 4.5 × 2.8 = 12.6 square metres. If camel milk sells at 1.5 times last month's price, and last month it was 20 shillings a cup, the new price is 20 × 1.5 = 30 shillings. Always estimate first so a misplaced point cannot slip past you: 4.5 × 2.8 is about 5 × 3 = 15, so 12.6 is reasonable while 126 or 1.26 would not be.

concepts.title: Dividing Decimals
concepts.explanation:
Division of decimals has two cases. When you divide by a whole number, keep the decimal point in the answer directly above the point in the number being divided, then divide as normal. For 12.6 ÷ 3, the point sits above, and 12 ÷ 3 = 4, 6 ÷ 3 = 2, giving 4.2. For 47.2 ÷ 8, long division gives 5.9.

When you divide by a decimal, first turn the divisor into a whole number by multiplying both numbers by the same power of 10. This does not change the answer, because you are multiplying top and bottom of a fraction by the same amount. For 8.4 ÷ 2.1, multiply both by 10 to get 84 ÷ 21 = 4. For 15.75 ÷ 0.25, multiply both by 100 to get 1575 ÷ 25 = 63. The rule is simple: shift the point in the divisor until it is whole, then shift the point in the dividend the same number of places.

Sometimes a division does not come out exactly, so you add trailing zeros to the dividend and keep going. For 7 ÷ 8, write 7.000 and divide to get 0.875. Other divisions never end – they produce a recurring decimal. For 1 ÷ 3 the threes repeat forever: 1 ÷ 3 = 0.333…, which we can write with a dot over the 3. Recognising when a division terminates and when it recurs is a useful skill you will meet again with fractions.
concepts.example: Dividing by powers of 10 is especially quick: dividing by 10 moves the point one place left (45.6 ÷ 10 = 4.56), and dividing by 100 moves it two places left (45.6 ÷ 100 = 0.456). Division is the operation behind unit rates and averages. If 3.5 kg of mangoes cost 875 shillings, the price per kilogram is 875 ÷ 3.5 = 250 shillings. If a 15.6 m rope is cut into 1.2 m pieces, the number of pieces is 15.6 ÷ 1.2 = 156 ÷ 12 = 13. As always, estimate to check: 15.6 ÷ 1.2 is about 15 ÷ 1 = 15, so 13 is in the right region.

concepts.title: Mental Calculation Strategies
concepts.explanation:
Because our number system is built on tens, decimals lend themselves beautifully to mental calculation. Learning a handful of strategies makes you faster and sharpens your feel for whether an answer is reasonable. Here are the most useful ones.

Rounding and adjusting. To add 4.7 + 2.8 in your head, round to 5 + 3 = 8, then adjust back. You added 0.3 too much to the first number and 0.2 too much to the second, so subtract 0.5 from 8 to get 7.5. The same works for subtraction: 8.3 − 2.7 rounds to 8 − 3 = 5, and adjusting gives 5.6.

Using fraction equivalents. Some decimals have friendly fraction twins. Since 0.5 = 1/2, multiplying by 0.5 is the same as halving: 16 × 0.5 = 16 ÷ 2 = 8. Since 0.25 = 1/4, 20 × 0.25 = 20 ÷ 4 = 5. And 0.1 = 1/10, so 0.1 × 47 = 4.7. Knowing these by heart turns awkward multiplications into simple divisions.

Partitioning (breaking numbers apart). For 3.6 × 4, split 3.6 into 3 + 0.6, multiply each part, then recombine: (3 × 4) + (0.6 × 4) = 12 + 2.4 = 14.4. Doubling and halving helps too: for 1.5 × 8, double 1.5 to 3 and halve 8 to 4, giving 3 × 4 = 12. Because you doubled one number and halved the other, the product is unchanged.

Compensation. When a number is close to a whole number, adjust it to make the multiplication easy, then correct. For 4.9 × 6, treat 4.9 as 5 − 0.1: (5 × 6) − (0.1 × 6) = 30 − 0.6 = 29.4. Pattern spotting is related: to multiply by 0.9, take the number minus a tenth of itself, so 0.9 × 7 = 7 − 0.7 = 6.3.
concepts.example: Clustering and front-end estimation help with long sums. When adding 2.1 + 2.3 + 1.9 + 2.2, notice every number is near 2, so the sum is about 4 × 2 = 8 (the exact answer is 8.5). Front-end estimation for 23.7 + 45.2 + 67.8 uses the leading digits: 20 + 40 + 60 = 120, close to the exact 136.7. These strategies are not about getting the exact answer – they are about knowing roughly what to expect so mistakes cannot hide. Choose whichever strategy best fits the numbers in front of you; with practice the choice becomes instant.

methods.title: How to order a set of decimals
steps: Write every number to the same number of decimal places using trailing zeros.
Compare the tenths digit of each number.
If tenths are equal, compare hundredths, then thousandths.
Write the numbers in order, smallest to largest.

methods.title: How to divide by a decimal
steps: Count the decimal places in the divisor.
Multiply both dividend and divisor by that power of 10.
The divisor is now a whole number – divide as usual.
Estimate to check the answer is reasonable.

methods.title: How to check any answer
steps: Round each number to something simple.
Do the easy calculation to get an estimate.
Compare your exact answer with the estimate.
If they are far apart, find and fix the mistake.

methods.title: Multiply two decimals
steps: Solution: Ignore the points: 67 × 84 = 5628.
Count decimal places: 6.7 has one and 8.4 has one, so the answer needs two.
Place the point: 56.28.
Estimate to check: 7 × 8 = 56, so 56.28 is right.

methods.title: Divide by a decimal
steps: Solution: Make the divisor whole by multiplying both numbers by 10: 896 ÷ 32.
Now divide: 32 × 20 = 640, remainder 256; 32 × 8 = 256, remainder 0.
Estimate: 90 ÷ 3 = 30, so 28 is sensible.

methods.title: A two-step problem
methods.example: A car travels at 65.5 km/h for 2.5 hours, then rests. How far does it travel?
steps: Solution: Distance = speed × time = 65.5 × 2.5.
Multiply 655 × 25 = 16375; with 1 + 1 = 2 decimal places the answer is 163.75 km.
Estimate: 66 × 2.5 = 165, so 163.75 is reasonable.

workedExamples.title: Order a set of decimals
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Write each to three decimal places: 0.450, 0.500, 0.405, 0.540. Compare tenths first: 0.405 has 4, and so does 0.450, while 0.500 has 5 and 0.540 has 5. Among the two starting with 4 tenths, 0.405 (0 hundredths) is less than 0.450 (5 hundredths). Among the two starting with 5 tenths, 0.500 is less than 0.540. So the order is 0.405, 0.45, 0.5, 0.54.

workedExamples.title: Add decimals of different lengths
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Line up the points and use trailing zeros: 0.75 + 0.90 + 1.25. Hundredths: 5 + 0 + 5 = 10, write 0 carry 1. Tenths: 7 + 9 + 2 + 1 = 19, write 9 carry 1. Ones: 0 + 0 + 1 + 1 = 2. The answer is 2.90 = 2.9.

workedExamples.title: Subtract from a whole number
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Write 15 as 15.000 so both numbers have three decimal places. Subtract with borrowing: 15.000 − 7.456 = 7.544. Check by adding back: 7.544 + 7.456 = 15.000. Correct.

workedExamples.title: Multiply two decimals
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Ignore the points: 67 × 84 = 5628. Count decimal places: 6.7 has one and 8.4 has one, so the answer needs two. Place the point: 56.28. Estimate to check: 7 × 8 = 56, so 56.28 is right.

workedExamples.title: Divide by a decimal
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Make the divisor whole by multiplying both numbers by 10: 896 ÷ 32. Now divide: 32 × 20 = 640, remainder 256; 32 × 8 = 256, remainder 0. So 896 ÷ 32 = 28. Estimate: 90 ÷ 3 = 30, so 28 is sensible.

workedExamples.title: A two-step problem
workedExamples.prompt: A car travels at 65.5 km/h for 2.5 hours, then rests. How far does it travel?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Distance = speed × time = 65.5 × 2.5. Multiply 655 × 25 = 16375; with 1 + 1 = 2 decimal places the answer is 163.75 km. Estimate: 66 × 2.5 = 165, so 163.75 is reasonable.

workedExamples.title: A mental-strategy calculation
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Recognise that 0.25 = 1/4, so 0.25 × 48 is the same as 48 ÷ 4 = 12. No written working needed – the fraction equivalent turns it into a quick division.

workedExamples.title: Combine operations with brackets
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Do the brackets first: 12.5 + 7.8 = 20.3. Then multiply: 20.3 × 2.4. Ignore points: 203 × 24 = 4872; with 1 + 1 = 2 decimal places the answer is 48.72. Estimate: 20 × 2.4 = 48, so 48.72 is correct.

activities.title: The Market Receipt
activities.materials: paper, pencil, and prices from a real or pretend shop.
steps: Choose five items and give each a decimal price in shillings, such as 12.45 or 7.80.
Add the prices carefully, lining up the decimal points, to find the total.
Estimate the total first by rounding each price, then compare with your exact answer.
Work out the change from a round note such as 50 or 100 shillings.
This trains the addition and subtraction you will use every time you shop.

activities.title: Decimal War (Comparing Game)
activities.materials: paper cards, each showing a decimal between 0 and 1 (write about 20 of them).
steps: Shuffle the cards and deal them equally between two players, face down.
Each player turns over one card at the same time.
The larger decimal wins both cards – write the > or < statement to prove it.
If they are equal (for example 0.5 and 0.50), each player turns over another card to break the tie.
The game trains you to compare tenths first, then hundredths – quickly and confidently.

activities.title: Kitchen Scaling Investigation
activities.materials: a simple recipe with measured amounts, and paper.
steps: Write down the ingredient amounts, such as 2.5 cups of flour and 0.75 cups of sugar.
Scale the recipe up by 1.5 times by multiplying each amount by 1.5.
Scale the recipe down to half by dividing each amount by 2.
Check that doubling your halved recipe returns the original amounts.

activities.title: Sports Statistics Project
activities.materials: results from a football match or a running race (real or made up).
steps: Record several race times to the hundredth of a second, such as 12.45 s.
Order the times from fastest to slowest.
Find the difference between the fastest and slowest times by subtracting.
Work out the average time by adding the times and dividing by how many there are.

activities.title: Mental Math Speed Round (Family Game)
activities.materials: your family or friends (or your AI tutor if no one is available), and a list of quick questions.
steps: One person reads out a question such as 0.5 × 24 or 0.25 × 16.
Everyone answers in their head and explains the strategy they used.
Award a point for the correct answer and a bonus point for the clearest explanation.
Take turns being the question-master and keep a running score.

activities.title: Build a Place-Value Grid
activities.materials: paper, a ruler, and a pencil.
steps: Draw a grid with columns headed ones, tenths, hundredths and thousandths.
Write five different decimals, one digit in each column.
For each number, say the value of every digit out loud.
Challenge a partner (or your AI tutor, if no one is available) to place a spoken number, such as 'three point four five', into the grid.

After your activities, talk or write about these questions: Which activity made decimals clearest for you? What was the trickiest part? Which operation – ordering, adding, subtracting, multiplying or dividing – do you still want more practice with? rules.title: Place Value Rule
rules.text: Each place after the point is one tenth of the place before it. 1st place = tenths, 2nd = hundredths, 3rd = thousandths. 0.5 is ten times larger than 0.05.

rules.title: Add and Subtract Rule
rules.text: Line up the decimal points, one under the other. Fill gaps with trailing zeros so every number is the same length. Bring the decimal point straight down into the answer.

rules.title: Multiply Rule
rules.text: Multiply as whole numbers, ignoring the points. Count the total decimal places in both factors. Give the answer that many decimal places.

rules.title: Divide Rule
rules.text: To divide by a decimal, multiply both numbers by the same power of 10. Keep multiplying until the divisor is a whole number. Then divide as normal, keeping the point in line.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A number multiplied by 0.25 gives 9. What is the number? Explain your reasoning.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The number is 9 ÷ 0.25 = 36, because 0.25 = 1/4 so we multiply 9 by 4.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain, with an example, why 0.45 is ten times larger than 0.045.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 0.45 = 45 hundredths and 0.045 = 45 thousandths; since a hundredth is ten times a thousandth, 0.45 is ten times 0.045.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Calculate 2.345 × 1.67 by multiplying whole numbers first, then placing the point. Check with an estimate.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 2345 × 167 = 391615; with 3 + 2 = 5 decimal places the answer is 3.91615 (estimate 2 × 1.67 ≈ 3.34, close).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Dividing Decimals.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Division of decimals has two cases. When dividing by a whole number, keep the decimal point in the answer directly above the point in the dividend, then divide as normal - for example, 12.6 ÷ 3 = 4.2. When dividing by a decimal, first convert the divisor into a whole number by multiplying both the dividend and the divisor by the same power of 10 (this does not change the answer, since it is the same as multiplying the top and bottom of a fraction by the same number). Then divide as normal - for example, 89.6 ÷ 3.2 becomes 896 ÷ 32 = 28.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Mental Calculation Strategies.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Because our number system is built on tens, decimals suit mental calculation well. Useful strategies include rounding and adjusting (e.g. 4.7 + 2.8 rounds to 5 + 3 = 8, then adjust back by 0.5 to get 7.5), using fraction equivalents (0.5 = 1/2, so 16 × 0.5 = 16 ÷ 2 = 8; 0.25 = 1/4, so 20 × 0.25 = 20 ÷ 4 = 5), and partitioning or compensation to split a calculation into easier parts.

I can use mental strategies – rounding and adjusting, fraction equivalents, partitioning, and compensation – to calculate efficiently.
I can estimate to check whether a calculated answer is sensible.
I can solve multi-step word problems involving decimals and interpret the answers in context.
